words: area; base; height; parallelogram; trapezoid; right triangle; polygon; compose; decompose; square unit
notes: IM 6.1 (Area and Surface Area), lessons 1 to 11; cluster 6.G.A, supporting (it practises the major expression work of 6.EE). Students find areas of parallelograms, all triangles (not only right ones), trapezoids and other polygons by cutting and rearranging into rectangles, by enclosing in a rectangle and subtracting, or by splitting into triangles, then name why A = bh for a parallelogram and A = (1/2)bh for a triangle work (any side can be the base; the height is perpendicular to it, and may fall outside the figure). Numbers: whole numbers, fractions and decimals in context; units are square units. Applies 6.EE.A.2c (evaluating the formulas at given values; owned by m6-expressions-variables). Limit: polygons only, no circles (grade 7). Progressions G K-6, PDF page 136 (printed 130) and Geometry 7-8, PDF page 222 (printed 216).

words: net; face; edge; vertex; prism; pyramid; surface area; squared; cubed
notes: IM 6.1, lessons 12 to 19; cluster 6.G.A, supporting. Students draw and fold nets made of rectangles and triangles for prisms and pyramids, match nets to solids, and use a net to find surface area as the sum of the face areas, in real problems (wrapping, painting). Introduces "squared" and "cubed" as exponents 2 and 3 for square and cubic units (6.EE.A.1, owned by m6-exponents, starts here as IM 6.1.17 does). Limit: faces are rectangles and triangles only; no formula for surface area is required, and no curved solids. New model name "net" (no shared name fits a flat pattern that folds into a solid). Progressions G K-6, PDF page 137 (printed 131).

words: ratio; for every; to; colon; quantity; batch
notes: IM 6.2 (Introducing Ratios), lessons 1 to 5; cluster 6.RP.A, major. Students describe a ratio between two quantities in words ("3 cups of flour for every 2 eggs", "3 to 2", "3 : 2"), draw discrete diagrams and tape diagrams, and see that doubling or tripling a recipe keeps the same ratio. Ratio notation is kept distinct from fraction notation on purpose (Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 164 (printed 158)). Numbers: whole-number quantities. Expected error: additive thinking (adding the same amount to both quantities). Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 163 (printed 157).

words: equivalent ratios; double number line; table; row; column; same rate; compare
notes: IM 6.2, lessons 6 to 16; cluster 6.RP.A, major. Students make equivalent ratios by multiplying both quantities by the same number, record them on double number lines and in ratio tables, find missing values, plot the pairs on the first-quadrant coordinate plane (they fall on a line through the origin) and use tables to compare two ratios (same shade of paint, same speed). Introduces the double-number-line (best when the units differ) and the ratio-table. The reasoning grows from repeated addition to scaling by multiplication and division (Progressions RP 6-7, PDF pages 166 to 167 (printed 160 to 161)). Limit: whole-number measurements in the tables; no proportion equations (cross multiplying is not required in grade 6, printed page 161).

words: part; whole; total; tape diagram; strategy
notes: IM 6.2, lessons 14 to 17 (part-part-whole and "solving more ratio problems"); cluster 6.RP.A, major. Owns the parent standard: students choose among tables, tape diagrams, double number lines and equations to solve ratio problems, including part-part-whole ("a 3 to 2 mix, 85 cups in all") with a tape diagram, and say why their choice fits. Lettered parts are owned by m6-equivalent-ratios (a), m6-unit-rate (b), m6-percent (c) and m6-unit-conversion (d). Numbers: whole numbers and simple fractions of a part. Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 168 (printed 162).

words: rate; unit rate; per; each; unit price; constant speed; best buy
cross_subject: science:MS-ESS2-2 (rates such as millimeters per year)
notes: IM 6.3 (Unit Rates and Percentages), lessons 5 to 9, and IM 6.2 speed lessons; cluster 6.RP.A, major. For a ratio a : b with b not 0, students find the two unit rates (a/b of the first per 1 of the second, and b/a the other way), use "per" and "for each 1", and solve unit price and constant speed problems ("7 hours to mow 4 lawns, how many lawns in 35 hours"). Unit rates are especially useful for finding entries (printed page 162). Limit: unit rates with non-complex fractions only (the standards footnote, Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 166 (printed 160)); rates of fractions per fractions wait for grade 7.

words: convert; unit; inch; foot; centimeter; meter; liter; kilogram; conversion rate
notes: IM 6.3, lessons 1 to 4; cluster 6.RP.A, major. Students treat "12 inches in a foot" or "1,000 grams in a kilogram" as a rate and convert with a double number line, a table or a unit rate, deciding whether the number should get bigger or smaller (smaller unit, more of them). Customary and metric units; whole-number and decimal measurements. Limit: one conversion at a time (no derived units such as square feet to square yards). Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 168 (printed 162).

words: percent; per hundred; of; whole; part; 100%
notes: IM 6.3, lessons 10 to 16; cluster 6.RP.A, major. A percent is a rate per 100: students find a percent of a quantity (30% of 60), find the whole given a part and the percent ("75% of the budget is $1200"), and find what percent one quantity is of another, on double number lines marked 0% to 100%, in tables and with tape diagrams; benchmark percents (10%, 25%, 50%, 75%) first. Limit: no percent increase or decrease, tax, tip or interest (grade 7). Progressions RP 6-7, PDF pages 164 and 168 (printed 158 and 162).

words: quotient; dividend; divisor; how many groups; how much in each group; reciprocal
notes: IM 6.4 (Dividing Fractions), lessons 1 to 14; cluster 6.NS.A, major. Students interpret a division of fractions as "how many groups of b in a" or "how much in one group", draw it with tape diagrams and area diagrams, connect it to the related multiplication (a / b = c because c x b = a), and reach the algorithm of multiplying by the reciprocal as a short cut they can explain. Word problems: "how much chocolate each person gets if 3 people share 1/2 lb", "how many 3/4-cup servings in 2/3 of a cup", "how wide is a land strip 3/4 mi long with area 1/2 square mi". Fractions by fractions now (grade 5 divided only unit fractions by whole numbers and back). Progressions NS 6-8, PDF pages 206 to 207 (printed 200 to 201).

words: volume; cubic unit; edge length; prism; V = lwh; V = bh
notes: IM 6.4, lessons 12 to 15 (and IM 6.1.15); cluster 6.G.A, supporting (it practises fraction multiplication and division of 6.NS.A). Students pack a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths with cubes of unit fraction edge (1/2 or 1/4 unit) and show the volume equals length x width x height, then use V = lwh and V = Bh with fractional edges, including finding a missing edge by dividing. Limit: right rectangular prisms only. Progressions G K-6, PDF page 137 (printed 131).

words: long division; dividend; divisor; quotient; remainder; partial quotients; standard algorithm
notes: IM 6.5 (Arithmetic in Base Ten), lessons 12 to 15; cluster 6.NS.B, additional. Fluency with the standard division algorithm for multi-digit whole numbers (this is the fluency grade for division; grade 5 used place value strategies and area models). Students link partial quotients and base-ten diagrams to the written steps, then practise to fluency with spaced mixed practice and no on-screen timer. Numbers: up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, remainders written as whole numbers, fractions or decimals as the context needs. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 207 (printed 201).

words: decimal; tenths; hundredths; thousandths; product; quotient; estimate; standard algorithm
notes: IM 6.5, lessons 1 to 11 and 13 to 15; cluster 6.NS.B, additional (but used in every later strand). Fluency with the standard algorithms to add, subtract, multiply and divide multi-digit decimals, explained by place value (base-ten diagrams, area diagrams for decimal products, multiplying dividend and divisor by the same power of ten before dividing). Contexts: money, measurements. Estimate first to check where the decimal point goes. Limit: grade 5 went to hundredths with strategies; here any number of places with the algorithm. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 207 (printed 201).

words: factor; multiple; common factor; greatest common factor; common multiple; least common multiple; distributive property
notes: IM 6.7 (Rational Numbers), lessons 16 to 18; cluster 6.NS.B, additional. Students find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers up to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers up to 12, in problems (equal bags, schedules that line up), and use the distributive property to write a sum of two whole numbers as a common factor times a sum (36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2)), drawn as a rectangle split in two. Limits as the standard sets them: GCF for numbers 1 to 100, LCM for numbers 1 to 12. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 208 (printed 202).

words: exponent; base; power; squared; cubed; order of operations
notes: IM 6.6 (Expressions and Equations), lessons 12 to 15, after IM 6.1.17; cluster 6.EE.A, major. Students write and evaluate numerical expressions with whole-number exponents (5^3, (1/2)^2, 0.2^3, 2 x 3^2), learn that the exponent applies only to the number it touches, and add exponents to the order of operations. Limit: whole-number exponents on whole-number, fraction and decimal bases; no negative or zero-exponent rules (grade 8). Hands on to grade 8 (m8-integer-exponents, m8-roots) across grade 7 on purpose: grade 7 has no exponent standard. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 180 (printed 174).

words: variable; expression; term; coefficient; sum; product; factor; quotient; evaluate; substitute
notes: IM 6.6, lessons 1 to 2 and 10 to 15, with IM 6.1 formula work and IM 6.7.2b; cluster 6.EE.A, major. Students write expressions that record operations with numbers and letters ("subtract y from 5" is 5 - y), name parts with sum, term, product, factor, quotient and coefficient, see 2(8 + 7) as a product of two factors, and evaluate expressions and formulas (V = s^3, A = 6s^2) at given values with the order of operations. Numbers: whole numbers, fractions and decimals, all nonnegative. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF pages 180 to 182 (printed 174 to 176).

words: equivalent; distributive property; like terms; expand; factor; commutative; associative
notes: IM 6.6, lessons 8 to 11; cluster 6.EE.A, major. Students use the properties of operations to write equivalent expressions (3(2 + x) = 6 + 3x; 24x + 18y = 6(4x + 3y); y + y + y = 3y), draw the distributive property as a rectangle with split side lengths, and test whether two expressions are equivalent by reasoning and by substituting values (equivalent means equal for every value of the letter). Limit: nonnegative numbers; linear expressions only; subtraction inside factored forms waits for grade 7. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 182 (printed 176).

words: equation; solution; solve; unknown; true; false; substitute; balanced
notes: IM 6.6, lessons 1 to 7; cluster 6.EE.B, major. Solving is answering "which values make this true?": students test values by substitution, write an equation from a tape diagram or a story with a letter for the unknown, and solve x + p = q and px = q by doing the same to both sides of a balanced hanger. Introduces the equation-balance (hanger diagram). Limit as the standard sets it: p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers (fractions and decimals allowed, no negatives); one-step forms only, two-step equations are grade 7. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF pages 182 to 183 (printed 176 to 177).

words: independent variable; dependent variable; relationship; table; graph; equation
cross_subject: science:MS-PS3-4 (temperature against time as two quantities that change together)
notes: IM 6.6, lessons 16 to 18; cluster 6.EE.C, major. Students use two letters for two quantities that change together (distance d and time t at a constant speed, cost c of n items), write an equation with the dependent variable alone on one side (d = 65t), and move between the equation, a table of values and a first-quadrant graph, saying which variable depends on which. Introduces the function-table (input and output columns), carried to grade 8 functions. Limit: relationships of the form y = kx and y = x + c, nonnegative values. Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 166 (printed 160) and EE 6-8, PDF page 184 (printed 178).

words: positive; negative; integer; rational number; opposite; zero; sea level; above; below
cross_subject: science:MS-PS1-4 (temperatures below zero as negative numbers); social-studies:ss6-timeline-deep-time (dates on either side of a zero point)
notes: IM 6.7 (Rational Numbers), lessons 1 to 3; cluster 6.NS.C, major. Positive and negative numbers name quantities in opposite directions (temperature, elevation, credit and debit, charge); 0 has a meaning in each context. Students extend the number line left of 0 (and below 0 on a vertical line), place integers, fractions and decimals, and see that the opposite of the opposite is the number itself (-(-3) = 3) and that 0 is its own opposite. Limit: placing and naming only; no operations with negative numbers (grade 7). Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 208 (printed 202).

words: greater than; less than; order; absolute value; distance from zero; magnitude
notes: IM 6.7, lessons 4 to 8; cluster 6.NS.C, major. Students read -3 > -7 as "-3 is to the right of -7", write and explain order statements in context (-3 degrees C is warmer than -7 degrees C), find |x| as the distance from 0, read absolute value as size of a debt or depth, and keep comparison of absolute values apart from order ("a balance less than -30 dollars is a debt greater than 30 dollars"). Expected error: thinking -7 > -3 because 7 > 3. Numbers: integers, fractions and decimals. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 209 (printed 203).

words: inequality; solution set; greater than; less than; at least; at most; infinitely many
notes: IM 6.7, lessons 9 to 10; cluster 6.EE.B, major. Students write x > c or x < c for a condition in a context (a ride needs riders taller than 48 inches), see that such an inequality has infinitely many solutions, and show the solutions on a number line with an open or closed circle and a ray. Limit: one-variable inequalities of the form x > c or x < c (including "or equal" for contexts); no solving of two-step inequalities (grade 7). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 183 (printed 177).

words: quadrant; ordered pair; x-coordinate; y-coordinate; origin; reflection; vertex; distance
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-mena-maps (points located by two signed coordinates)
notes: IM 6.7, lessons 11 to 15; clusters 6.NS.C, major, and 6.G.A, supporting. Students extend the coordinate plane to four quadrants, read the signs of an ordered pair as its quadrant, see that (3, 5) and (-3, 5) are reflections across the y-axis, solve problems by plotting points (maps, temperatures over time), and find the distance between two points with the same first or second coordinate using absolute value. They draw polygons from vertex coordinates and find side lengths that way (6.G.A.3). Limit: distances along horizontal or vertical lines only (diagonal distance is grade 8). Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 209 (printed 203); G K-6, PDF page 137 (printed 131).

words: statistical question; variability; data; distribution; center; spread; shape
cross_subject: ela:W.6.7 (a short investigation that answers a question with gathered information)
notes: IM 6.8 (Data Sets and Distributions), lessons 1 to 5; cluster 6.SP.A, additional. Students tell a statistical question (one that expects varied answers, "how old are the students in my school?") from one that does not ("how old am I?"), gather data to answer one, and describe the resulting distribution by its center, spread and overall shape (symmetric, skewed, peaks, gaps, clusters) on a dot plot. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 193 (printed 187).

words: dot plot; histogram; bin; frequency; box plot; quartile; five-number summary
notes: IM 6.8, lessons 6 to 8 and 15 to 16; cluster 6.SP.B, additional. Students display numerical data on a number line as dot plots, histograms (equal-width bins, bars touching, frequency on the vertical axis) and box plots (minimum, quartiles, median, maximum), and choose the display that suits the data set (histograms for large data sets). Introduces the histogram and box-plot. Limit: numerical data on one variable. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 193 (printed 187).

words: mean; median; mean absolute deviation; interquartile range; range; measure of center; measure of variability
cross_subject: science:MS-PS3-3 (summarize repeated trial data with a measure of center)
notes: IM 6.8, lessons 9 to 16; cluster 6.SP.A and 6.SP.B, additional. A measure of center sums up a data set in one number and a measure of variability says how the values vary in one number. Students find the mean (as fair share and as balance point), the median, the mean absolute deviation and the interquartile range, and describe patterns and striking departures (outliers). Uses the grade 6 decimal fluency of m6-decimal-operations for the arithmetic. Limit: data sets small enough to compute by hand. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF pages 193 to 194 (printed 187 to 188).

words: observation; attribute; unit of measure; symmetric; skewed; outlier; summary
notes: IM 6.8, lessons 12 to 18, and IM 6.9 (Putting it All Together); cluster 6.SP.B, additional. Students write a full summary of a numerical data set in context: how many observations, what was measured and how and in what units, the center and variability, and why median and IQR suit a skewed set or one with outliers while mean and MAD suit a roughly symmetric one. Ends with a short data project. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 194 (printed 188).

words: scale drawing; scaled copy; scale factor; scale; corresponding; actual length
cross_subject: social-studies:ss6-mena-maps (a map scale is a scale drawing)
notes: IM 7.1 (Scale Drawings), all lessons; cluster 7.G.A, additional (it practises the ratio reasoning of 7.RP.A). Students make and recognise scaled copies (every length multiplied by the same scale factor, angles unchanged), use a scale such as "1 cm represents 5 m" or "1 to 500" to find actual lengths and areas from a drawing, see that areas scale by the square of the scale factor, and redraw a drawing at a new scale. Numbers: whole numbers, fractions and decimals. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 225 (printed 219); RP 6-7, PDF page 172 (printed 166).

words: proportional relationship; constant of proportionality; unit rate; for every; not proportional
cross_subject: science:MS-ETS1-4 (testing whether one quantity is proportional to another)
notes: IM 7.2 (Introducing Proportional Relationships), lessons 1 to 6; cluster 7.RP.A, major. Students decide whether two quantities are proportional by testing for a constant unit rate in a table (ages of two people are not; people and hours to paint a fence are not), and identify the constant of proportionality in tables, diagrams and words. Owns the parent 7.RP.A.2 with m7-proportional-equations (c) and m7-proportional-graphs (d and the graph test of a). Progressions RP 6-7, PDF pages 169 to 170 (printed 163 to 164).

words: equation; constant of proportionality; y = kx; dependent; independent
notes: IM 7.2, lessons 7 to 10; cluster 7.RP.A, major. Students write y = kx for a proportional relationship (t = pn for total cost of n items at price p), find k from a table or a description, and see that the relationship can be written both ways (k and 1/k). The constant of proportionality replaces the traditional "set up a proportion and cross multiply" method, which hides the unit rate (Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 170 (printed 164)). Numbers: rational, nonnegative.

words: origin; straight line; point; unit rate; steepness
notes: IM 7.2, lessons 11 to 15; cluster 7.RP.A, major. Students graph proportional relationships, recognise them as straight lines through the origin (the graph test of 7.RP.A.2a), and explain what a point (x, y) means in the situation, with special attention to (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate. Compares several relationships on one set of axes (steeper means a greater unit rate). Limit: first quadrant, nonnegative values; slope as a word waits for grade 8. Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 170 (printed 164).

words: complex fraction; unit rate; per; ratio of fractions
notes: IM 7.4 (Proportional Relationships and Percentages), lessons 1 to 3, and IM 7.2; cluster 7.RP.A, major. Students compute unit rates from ratios of fractions ("1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour" is 2 miles per hour), including lengths, areas and quantities in like or different units, using tables and fraction division. This lifts the grade 6 limit to non-complex fractions. Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 169 (printed 163).

words: circle; radius; diameter; circumference; pi; area of a circle; approximate
notes: IM 7.3 (Measuring Circles), all lessons; cluster 7.G.B, additional. Students measure many circles, graph circumference against diameter and find a proportional relationship with constant pi (this applies 7.RP.A.2a), then know C = pi d = 2 pi r and A = pi r^2, giving an informal derivation of the area by cutting a circle into wedges and rearranging into a near-parallelogram of base half the circumference and height r. Area is not proportional to radius. Values of pi: 3.14, 22/7 or left as pi. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 227 (printed 221).

words: percent increase; percent decrease; tax; tip; discount; markup; interest; commission; percent error
cross_subject: science:MS-ESS3-4 (percent increase in population and use); social-studies:ss7-roman-economy (percent increase and tax rates)
notes: IM 7.4, lessons 5 to 17; cluster 7.RP.A, major. Students solve multistep ratio and percent problems: simple interest, sales tax, markups and markdowns, tips, commission, fees, percent increase and decrease and percent error, seeing "a 5% increase" as multiplying by 1.05 (the expression link is owned by m7-linear-expressions). Double number lines and tape diagrams carry the reasoning before equations. Limit: simple interest only, no compound growth (high school). Progressions RP 6-7, PDF page 171 (printed 165). Teacher note: money contexts stay neutral; no student shares family income or debt.

words: additive inverse; opposite; sum; difference; zero pair; distance; integer
cross_subject: social-studies:ss7-time-zones (adding and subtracting signed numbers of hours); science:MS-PS1-4 (temperature changes across zero)
notes: IM 7.5 (Rational Number Arithmetic), lessons 1 to 7; cluster 7.NS.A, major. Students describe situations where opposites combine to 0, show p + q as a move of |q| from p on a number line (right for positive q, left for negative q), see subtraction as adding the opposite (p - q = p + (-q)) and the distance between two numbers as |p - q|, and use properties of operations as strategies. Numbers: integers, fractions and decimals, positive and negative. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF pages 210 to 211 (printed 204 to 205).

words: product; quotient; sign; negative times negative; property; rational number
notes: IM 7.5, lessons 8 to 12; cluster 7.NS.A, major. Students extend multiplication to signed numbers so the properties still hold (the distributive property forces (-1)(-1) = 1), use speed and direction contexts on a number line, learn that a quotient of integers with nonzero divisor is rational and that -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q), and use properties as strategies. Numbers: integers, fractions and decimals. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF pages 212 to 213 (printed 206 to 207).

words: terminating decimal; repeating decimal; long division; bar notation
notes: IM 7.4.4 and 7.5.12; cluster 7.NS.A, major. Students convert a fraction to a decimal by long division and see why the decimal either ends in 0s or repeats (the remainders can only take so many values), writing repeating decimals with a bar (1/3 = 0.333..., 2/11 = 0.1818...). Prepares grade 8 irrational numbers. Progressions NS 6-8, PDF page 214 (printed 208).

words: multistep; estimate; reasonable; mental math; convert; rational number
notes: IM 7.5, lessons 13 to 16, and IM 7.6; clusters 7.NS.A and 7.EE.B, major. Students solve multistep real problems with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, decimals, percents), converting between forms as needed, and check answers by mental estimation ("a $25 an hour worker gets a 10% raise, so $2.50 more"). Tools are chosen with purpose (calculator after estimating). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 185 (printed 179); NS 6-8, PDF page 213 (printed 207).

words: linear expression; expand; factor; combine like terms; rational coefficient; equivalent
notes: IM 7.6 (Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities), lessons 17 to 22; cluster 7.EE.A, major. Students add, subtract, factor and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients, including subtraction and negative coefficients (6 - 2(x - 3) = 12 - 2x), using the area model for the distributive property, and rewrite expressions to show meaning in a context (a + 0.05a = 1.05a means "increase by 5%" is "multiply by 1.05"). Expected error: distributing a negative to only the first term. Limit: linear expressions only. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 185 (printed 179).

words: equation; px + q = r; p(x + q) = r; solve; inverse operation; fluently
notes: IM 7.6, lessons 1 to 12; cluster 7.EE.B, major. Students construct simple equations from word problems, draw them as tape diagrams and hangers, and solve px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently, comparing the algebraic solution with an arithmetic one (subtract, then divide) and naming the operations in each. Numbers p, q, r are specific rational numbers, negatives allowed. Fluency is built with spaced mixed practice and no on-screen timer. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 186 (printed 180).

words: inequality; solution set; boundary; reverse the inequality; graph
notes: IM 7.6, lessons 13 to 16; cluster 7.EE.B, major. Students solve word problems leading to px + q > r or px + q < r, graph the solution set on a number line and interpret it in context ("you need at least 6 more sales"), and learn by testing values why multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality. Numbers p, q, r are specific rational numbers. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 187 (printed 181).

words: supplementary; complementary; vertical angles; adjacent; straight angle; unknown angle
notes: IM 7.7 (Angles, Triangles, and Prisms), lessons 1 to 5; cluster 7.G.B, additional (it practises the equation work of 7.EE.B). Students use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical and adjacent angles in multistep problems, writing and solving simple equations for an unknown angle (2x + 30 = 180). Angle measure itself is grade 4 (cross-band, see edges). Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 227 (printed 221).

words: construct; protractor; compass; unique triangle; triangle inequality; given conditions
notes: IM 7.7, lessons 6 to 10; cluster 7.G.A, additional. Students draw shapes with given conditions freehand, with ruler and protractor and with geometry software, focusing on triangles from three side lengths or three angle measures: noticing when the conditions give one triangle, more than one, or none (three lengths must satisfy the triangle inequality; three angles fix a shape but not a size). Prepares grade 8 congruence. Uses no carried model; tools are physical. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 225 (printed 219).

words: cross section; slice; plane; prism; pyramid; base; face
notes: IM 7.7, lessons 11 to 12; cluster 7.G.A, additional. Students describe the two-dimensional figures made by slicing right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids with a plane (parallel to the base, perpendicular to it, at a slant), building with clay or foam and checking with drawings. Limit: those two solids as the standard names. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 226 (printed 220).

words: composite figure; right prism; base; volume; surface area; cross section
notes: IM 7.7, lessons 13 to 17, and IM 7.9; cluster 7.G.B, additional. Students solve real problems with area of composite figures made of triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons, and with volume and surface area of cubes and right prisms with any polygon base (V = Bh, base area times height; surface area from a net). Limit: polygons and right prisms only; cylinders, cones and spheres are grade 8. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 226 (printed 220).

words: chance; probability; likely; unlikely; certain; impossible; outcome; event; relative frequency; long run
notes: IM 7.8 (Probability and Sampling), lessons 1 to 5; cluster 7.SP.C, supporting (it practises fractions, decimals and percents of 7.NS and 7.RP). Probability is a number from 0 to 1 placed on a number line (about 1/2 is neither likely nor unlikely). Students run chance experiments, find the relative frequency of an event over many trials, and predict ("a 6 on about 200 of 1,200 rolls"), seeing the relative frequency settle as trials grow. No in-band prerequisite: it rests on fractions, decimals and percents as numbers from grades 4 to 6 (m6-percent for the percent form). Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 196 (printed 190).

words: probability model; equally likely; sample space; uniform; observed frequency; expected
notes: IM 7.8, lessons 4 to 8; cluster 7.SP.C, supporting. Students build uniform probability models (a fair number cube, a name drawn from a class) and models from observed frequencies (a dropped paper cup landing open-end down), find probabilities of events from them, and compare a model with observed results, explaining a poor fit. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 197 (printed 191).

words: compound event; sample space; organized list; tree diagram; simulation; trial
notes: IM 7.8, lessons 6 to 10; cluster 7.SP.C, supporting. The probability of a compound event is the fraction of the sample space where it happens. Students list sample spaces with organized lists, tables and tree diagrams (introduced here), find the outcomes that make up "rolling double sixes", and design and run simulations (random digits, spinners) for events too awkward to list. Limit: no formal multiplication rule or independence (high school). Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 197 (printed 191).

words: population; sample; random sample; representative; biased; inference; estimate; margin
notes: IM 7.8, lessons 11 to 17; cluster 7.SP.A, supporting (it practises proportional reasoning: a sample proportion scaled to the population). Students learn that a sample tells about a population only if it is representative, that random sampling tends to give representative samples, and use data from a random sample to estimate a population mean or proportion, generating many samples of the same size to see how much estimates vary. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF pages 197 to 198 (printed 191 to 192).

words: overlap; difference in centers; mean absolute deviation; compare; inference; population
notes: IM 7.8, lessons 12 to 15; cluster 7.SP.B, additional. Students judge the visual overlap of two distributions with similar spread and express the difference in centers as a multiple of a measure of variability (centers 2 MADs apart is a meaningful difference), then use centers and variability from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations (are seventh-grade books longer than fourth-grade books?). Limit: informal only, no formal tests. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 199 (printed 193).

words: translation; rotation; reflection; rigid transformation; image; center of rotation; line of reflection
notes: IM 8.1 (Rigid Transformations and Congruence), lessons 1 to 10; cluster 8.G.A, major. Students move figures with tracing paper, grids and geometry software and verify by experiment that translations, rotations and reflections take lines to lines, segments to segments of the same length, angles to angles of the same measure and parallel lines to parallel lines. Introduces the transformation model. Limit: verifying by experiment, not formal proof (high school). Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 228 (printed 222).

words: coordinates; image; preimage; (x, y) to (x + a, y + b); dilation; scale factor; center
notes: IM 8.1, lessons 6 to 7, and IM 8.2, lessons 1 to 5; cluster 8.G.A, major. Students describe translations, rotations of 90 and 180 degrees about the origin, reflections across the axes and dilations from the origin by their effect on coordinates ((x, y) to (-x, y); (x, y) to (kx, ky)). Builds on grade 7 scale factors and the grade 6 four-quadrant plane. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF pages 228 to 229 (printed 222 to 223).

words: congruent; sequence of transformations; corresponding; map onto
notes: IM 8.1, lessons 11 to 14; cluster 8.G.A, major. Two figures are congruent when a sequence of rotations, reflections and translations takes one onto the other; given two congruent figures, students describe such a sequence, and explain why figures with different side lengths or angles cannot be congruent. Replaces "same size and shape" with a definition. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 228 (printed 222).

words: transversal; alternate interior angles; corresponding angles; angle sum; exterior angle; angle-angle
notes: IM 8.1, lessons 14 to 16, and IM 8.2, lessons 6 to 9; cluster 8.G.A, major. Students give informal arguments, using rigid transformations, for the angle sum of a triangle (180 degrees), the exterior angle, the angles made when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similar triangles (with m8-dilations-similarity). Limit: informal arguments, not two-column proof. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF pages 229 to 230 (printed 223 to 224).

words: dilation; center of dilation; scale factor; similar; similarity transformation
notes: IM 8.2 (Dilations, Similarity, and Introducing Slope), lessons 1 to 9; cluster 8.G.A, major. Two figures are similar when a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations and dilations takes one onto the other; students describe such a sequence and use it to find unknown lengths. Grade 7 scale drawings become dilations with a center. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 229 (printed 223).

words: slope; rise; run; slope triangle; y = mx; y = mx + b; intercept
notes: IM 8.2, lessons 10 to 12, and IM 8.3 (Linear Relationships), lessons 5 to 11; cluster 8.EE.B, major. Students use similar slope triangles to explain why the slope is the same between any two points on a non-vertical line, then derive y = mx for a line through the origin and y = mx + b for a line crossing the vertical axis at b. Introduces the graph-of-function name for a line read as a relationship. Negative slopes and lines through all four quadrants. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 189 (printed 183); Geometry 7-8, PDF page 229 (printed 223).

words: slope; unit rate; proportional; compare; representation
notes: IM 8.3, lessons 1 to 4; cluster 8.EE.B, major. Students graph proportional relationships and read the unit rate as the slope, then compare two proportional relationships shown in different ways (a distance-time graph against a distance-time equation: which moves faster?). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 189 (printed 183).

words: linear relationship; rate of change; initial value; vertical intercept; horizontal line; vertical line
notes: IM 8.3, lessons 5 to 14; cluster 8.F.A and 8.F.B, major. Before the word function, students meet non-proportional linear relationships (a cup stack starting at 6 cm, growing 1.5 cm per cup), read the rate of change and the starting amount from a context, a table and a graph, write y = mx + b, and see that the solutions of an equation in two variables (5x + 2y = 20) make a line. Starts 8.F.B.4 and 8.F.A.3, which m8-function-model and m8-function-compare own once IM 8.5 names functions. Progressions Functions 8, PDF page 244 (printed 238).

words: one solution; no solution; infinitely many solutions; collect like terms; distributive property; variable on both sides
notes: IM 8.4 (Linear Equations and Linear Systems), lessons 1 to 9; cluster 8.EE.C, major. Students solve linear equations in one variable with rational coefficients, including variables on both sides and expanding with the distributive property (3(x - 2) + 4 = 2x - 1/2), and classify equations as having one solution, no solution (x = a, a not b, as 3 = 5) or infinitely many (a = a) by transforming them into simpler forms. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 189 (printed 183).

words: system of equations; simultaneous; point of intersection; substitution; no solution; parallel lines
notes: IM 8.4, lessons 10 to 16; cluster 8.EE.C, major. The solution of a system of two linear equations in two variables is the point where the graphs cross, because that point satisfies both. Students estimate solutions by graphing, solve algebraically (substitution), solve simple cases by inspection (3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6 have no solution), and solve real problems that lead to two equations. Limit: elimination as a named method is not required (high school A-REI.C.5). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 190 (printed 184). (Assumes m7-two-step-equations rather than an in-grade row; m8-linear-equations is taught first within grade 8.)

words: function; input; output; exactly one; ordered pair; graph of a function
notes: IM 8.5 (Functions and Volume), lessons 1 to 4; cluster 8.F.A, major. A function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output; its graph is the set of ordered pairs (input, output). Students decide whether a table, a rule or a situation is a function, and read inputs and outputs from graphs. Limit: function notation f(x) is not required in grade 8 (high school F-IF.A.2). Progressions Functions 8, PDF page 243 (printed 237).

words: linear function; nonlinear; rate of change; compare; representation
notes: IM 8.5, lessons 5 to 9; cluster 8.F.A, major. Students compare two functions each shown a different way (a table and an equation: which has the greater rate of change?), interpret y = mx + b as a linear function whose graph is a straight line, and give examples of functions that are not linear (A = s^2 is not, since (1,1), (2,4), (3,9) are not on a line). Progressions Functions 8, PDF page 243 (printed 237).

words: model; rate of change; initial value; slope; intercept; linear function
notes: IM 8.5, lessons 9 to 11, with IM 8.3; cluster 8.F.B, major. Students construct a linear function to model a relationship, find the rate of change and initial value from a description, from two (x, y) values or from a table or graph, and interpret both in terms of the situation. Progressions Functions 8, PDF page 244 (printed 238).

words: increasing; decreasing; constant; linear; nonlinear; sketch
cross_subject: science:MS-PS3-1 (describe a relationship from the shape of its graph)
notes: IM 8.5, lessons 4 to 6 and 10 to 11; cluster 8.F.B, major. Students describe a functional relationship from a graph (where it increases or decreases, where it is linear or not) and sketch a graph from a verbal description (water filling a tank, a bike ride with a rest stop). Qualitative only, no formulas needed. Progressions Functions 8, PDF page 244 (printed 238).

words: cylinder; cone; sphere; hemisphere; radius; volume; pi
notes: IM 8.5, lessons 12 to 21; cluster 8.G.C, additional. Students know and use the volume formulas for cylinders (pi r^2 h), cones (one third of the cylinder with the same base and height) and spheres (4/3 pi r^3) in real problems, building from grade 7 base-times-height volume and circle area, and graph how volume changes with radius or height (linking to functions). Limit: formulas known, not derived formally. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 231 (printed 225).

words: scatter plot; association; positive; negative; linear; nonlinear; cluster; outlier; line of fit
cross_subject: science:MS-LS1-5 (scatter plots of growth against a condition)
notes: IM 8.6 (Associations in Data), lessons 1 to 8; cluster 8.SP.A, supporting (it practises the linear functions of 8.F). Students make and read scatter plots of bivariate measurement data, describe clustering, outliers, positive or negative and linear or nonlinear association, and informally fit a straight line where the association looks linear, judging the fit by how close the points are to it. Introduces the scatter-plot. Limit: lines fit by eye, no least squares (high school). Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 200 (printed 194).

words: linear model; slope; intercept; predict; interpret
notes: IM 8.6, lessons 5 to 8; cluster 8.SP.A, supporting. Students use the equation of a fitted linear model to answer questions and interpret its slope and intercept in context ("a slope of 1.5 cm per hour means each extra hour of sunlight goes with about 1.5 cm more plant growth"). Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 200 (printed 194).

words: two-way table; categorical data; frequency; relative frequency; row; column; association
notes: IM 8.6, lessons 9 to 10; cluster 8.SP.A, supporting. Students build two-way tables of frequencies and relative frequencies for two categorical variables on the same subjects (curfew and chores), compute row or column relative frequencies, and decide whether the two variables seem associated. Introduces the two-way-table. Progressions SP 6-8, PDF page 200 (printed 194). Teacher note: survey questions avoid personal or sensitive topics.

words: exponent; power; integer exponent; zero exponent; negative exponent; product of powers; power of a power
notes: IM 8.7 (Exponents and Scientific Notation), lessons 1 to 8; cluster 8.EE.A, major. Students develop and use the properties of integer exponents (3^2 x 3^-5 = 3^-3 = 1/27), explaining 10^0 = 1 and 10^-n = 1/10^n from patterns of repeated factors and place value, and write equivalent numerical expressions. Skips grade 7 on purpose: grade 7 has no exponent standard, so m6-exponents is the last place exponents are taught. Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 188 (printed 182).

words: scientific notation; power of ten; estimate; order of magnitude; times as much
cross_subject: science:MS-ESS1-3 (powers of ten for very large distances and sizes)
notes: IM 8.7, lessons 9 to 16; cluster 8.EE.A, major. Students estimate very large and very small quantities as a single digit times a power of ten (the population of the United States as 3 x 10^8) and say how many times as much one is than another, then operate with numbers in scientific notation, mixing decimal and scientific forms, choose sensible units (millimeters per year for sea-floor spreading), and read calculator output (3E8). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 188 (printed 182).

words: square root; cube root; perfect square; perfect cube; radical; irrational
notes: IM 8.8 (Pythagorean Theorem and Irrational Numbers), lessons 3 to 5 and 13 to 14; cluster 8.EE.A, major. Students use square root and cube root symbols for solutions of x^2 = p and x^3 = p (p a positive rational), drawing a square of given area and asking its side, evaluate roots of small perfect squares and cubes, and know that the square root of 2 is irrational. Limit as the standard sets it: small perfect squares and cubes. Skips grade 7 on purpose (no exponent or root standard there). Progressions EE 6-8, PDF page 188 (printed 182).

words: irrational number; rational number; decimal expansion; repeating; approximate; real number
notes: IM 8.8, lessons 3 to 5 and 13 to 15; cluster 8.NS.A, supporting. Numbers that are not rational are irrational. Every number has a decimal expansion; students show a repeating decimal is rational by turning it back into a fraction (0.1818... = 2/11), use rational approximations to compare irrationals and place them on a number line (square root of 2 is between 1.4 and 1.5, then between 1.41 and 1.42), and estimate expressions such as pi^2. Progressions NS 6-8; N, HS, PDF pages 215 to 216 (printed 209 to 210).

words: Pythagorean theorem; converse; hypotenuse; leg; right triangle; proof
notes: IM 8.8, lessons 6 to 10; cluster 8.G.B, major. Students explain a proof of the Pythagorean theorem and its converse by rearranging squares and triangles (an area argument), then find unknown side lengths of right triangles in real and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions (the diagonal of a box). Answers may be irrational and are left as roots or approximated. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF pages 230 to 231 (printed 224 to 225).

words: distance; coordinate; right triangle; hypotenuse; horizontal; vertical
notes: IM 8.8, lesson 11; cluster 8.G.B, major. Students find the distance between two points in the coordinate plane by drawing the right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical distances (|x2 - x1| and |y2 - y1|, the grade 7 distance as absolute difference) and applying the Pythagorean theorem. Limit: no distance formula is required as a memorised formula. Progressions Geometry 7-8, PDF page 231 (printed 225).
